ALI-HKG-2022:S11: Then, the data center infrastructure provider notified the chiller manufacturer.
ALI-HKG-2022:S13: At 10:30, we began to reduce loads on the computing, storage, network, database, and big data clusters of the entire data center to prevent the temperature from rising too fast and causing a fire.
ALI-HKG-2022:S15: At 12:30, the chiller manufacturer's engineers arrived on site.
ALI-HKG-2022:S16: After diagnosing the issue, on-site engineers decided to manually recirculate the water and discharge gas from the cooling tower, condenser water pipes, and cooling system condensers, but the chillers still did not resume stable operation.
ALI-HKG-2022:S17: Our engineers shut down the servers in rooms with high temperature.
ALI-HKG-2022:S18: At 14:47, the fire sprinkler system of a room was triggered automatically due to high temperature, which increased the difficulty in troubleshooting.
ALI-HKG-2022:S19: At 15:20, the chiller manufacturer's engineers manually adjusted system configurations to unbind the chillers from the cluster and individually restart each chiller.
ALI-HKG-2022:S20: The first chiller was restored and the temperature began to drop.
ALI-HKG-2022:S22: At 18:55, all four chillers were restored.
ALI-HKG-2022:S3: At 08:56 on December 18, 2022, we were alerted to rising corridor temperatures in data center rooms in Zone C of the China (Hong Kong) region.
ALI-HKG-2022:S4: Our engineers immediately started to inspect the situation and notified the data center infrastructure provider.
ALI-HKG-2022:S5: At 09:01, alerts on rising temperatures of multiple server rooms were generated, and the on-site engineers identified the issue as being due to a malfunction of the data center's chillers.
ALI-HKG-2022:S6: At 09:09, the data center infrastructure provider's engineers switched the four malfunctioning chillers over to the standby chillers and restarted the chillers based on the contingency plan.
ALI-HKG-2022:S7: However, these measures did not take effect.
ALI-HKG-2022:S72: Issue analysis: Air entered the cooling system of the data center due to lack of water, which affected the water circulation of the four active chillers.
ALI-HKG-2022:S73: However, the four standby chillers used the same water circulation system as the four active chillers, so the failover failed.
ALI-HKG-2022:S74: After recirculating the water and discharging gas, chillers could not be restarted individually because all chillers of the data center were bound into a cluster.
ALI-HKG-2022:S75: In this case, engineers had to manually modify the configurations of the chillers to allow them to run individually.
ALI-HKG-2022:S76: Then, the chillers were restarted one after another, which slowed the restoration progress of the entire cooling system.
ALI-HKG-2022:S77: It took 3 hours and 34 minutes to locate the cause, 2 hours and 57 minutes to recirculate the water and bleed the air from the equipment, and 3 hours and 32 minutes to unbind the four chillers from the cluster.
ALI-HKG-2022:S78: Corrective action: We will perform comprehensive checks on the infrastructure control systems of data centers.
ALI-HKG-2022:S79: We will expand the scope of metrics we monitor to obtain more fine-grained data and to ensure more efficient troubleshooting.
ALI-HKG-2022:S8: At 09:17, on-site engineers implemented the contingency plan for cooling failure in accordance to the issue handling process, and took auxiliary heat dissipation and ventilation measures accordingly.
ALI-HKG-2022:S80: We will also ensure that automatic failover and manual failover are both effective to avoid disaster recovery failures due to deadlocks.
ALI-HKG-2022:S82: Issue analysis: With the failure of the cooling system, the temperatures in all server rooms rose uncontrollably.
ALI-HKG-2022:S83: This triggered the fire sprinkler system, and water got into multiple power supply cabinets and server racks, damaging hardware and complicating the equipment restoration process.
ALI-HKG-2022:S84: Corrective action: We will strengthen the management of data center infrastructure providers, improve our contingency plan for data center cooling issues, and regularly conduct emergency response drills.
ALI-HKG-2022:S85: The contingency plan will include standardized emergency response processes and clarify when servers must be shut down and server rooms must be powered off.

AWS-NRT-2019:S10: It took longer to recover these instances and volumes and some needed to be retired as a result of failures to the underlying hardware.
AWS-NRT-2019:S18: This event was caused by a failure of our datacenter control system, which is used to control and optimize the various cooling systems used in our datacenters.
AWS-NRT-2019:S19: The control system runs on multiple hosts for high availability.
AWS-NRT-2019:S20: This control system contains third-party code which allows it to communicate with third-party devices such as fans, chillers, and temperature sensors.
AWS-NRT-2019:S21: It communicates either directly or through embedded Programmable Logic Controllers (PLC) which in turn communicate with the actual devices.
AWS-NRT-2019:S22: Just prior to the event, the datacenter control system was in the process of failing away from one of the control hosts.
AWS-NRT-2019:S23: During this kind of failover, the control system has to exchange information with other control systems and the datacenter equipment it controls (e.g., the cooling equipment and temperature sensors throughout the datacenter) to ensure that the new control host has the most up-to-date information about the state of the datacenter.
AWS-NRT-2019:S24: Due to a bug in the third-party control system logic, this exchange resulted in excessive interactions between the control system and the devices in the datacenter which ultimately resulted in the control system becoming unresponsive.
AWS-NRT-2019:S25: Our datacenters are designed such that if the datacenter control system fails, the cooling systems go into maximum cooling mode until the control system functionality is restored.
AWS-NRT-2019:S26: While this worked correctly in most of the datacenter, in a small portion of the datacenter, the cooling system did not correctly transition to this safe cooling configuration and instead shut down.
AWS-NRT-2019:S27: As an added safeguard, our datacenter operators have the ability to bypass the datacenter control systems and put our cooling system in “purge” mode to quickly exhaust hot air in the event of a malfunction.
AWS-NRT-2019:S28: The team attempted to activate purge in the affected areas of the datacenter, but this also failed.
AWS-NRT-2019:S29: At this point, temperatures began to rise in the affected part of the datacenter and servers began to power off when they became too hot.
AWS-NRT-2019:S3: Beginning at 12:36 PM JST, a small percentage of EC2 servers in a single Availability Zone in the Tokyo (AP-NORTHEAST-1) Region shut down due to overheating.
AWS-NRT-2019:S30: Because the datacenter control system was unavailable, the operations team had minimum visibility into the health and state of the datacenter cooling systems.
AWS-NRT-2019:S31: To recover, the team had to manually investigate and reset all of the affected pieces of equipment and put them into a maximum cooling configuration.
AWS-NRT-2019:S32: During this process, it was discovered that the PLCs controlling some of the air handling units were also unresponsive.
AWS-NRT-2019:S33: These controllers needed to be reset.
AWS-NRT-2019:S34: It was the failure of these PLC controllers which prevented the default cooling and “purge” mode from correctly working.
AWS-NRT-2019:S35: After these controllers were reset, cooling was restored to the affected area of the datacenter and temperatures began to decrease.
AWS-NRT-2019:S36: We are still working with our third-party vendors to understand the bug, and subsequent interactions, that caused both the control system and the impacted PLCs to become unresponsive.
AWS-NRT-2019:S37: In the interim, we have disabled the failover mode that triggered this bug on our control systems to ensure we do not have a recurrence of this issue.
AWS-NRT-2019:S38: We have also trained our local operations teams to quickly identify and remediate this situation if it were to recur, and we are confident that we could reset the system before seeing any customer impact if a similar situation was to occur for any reason.
AWS-NRT-2019:S39: Finally, we are working to modify the way that we control the impacted air handling units to ensure that “purge mode” is able to bypass the PLC controllers completely.
AWS-NRT-2019:S40: This is an approach we have begun using in our newest datacenter designs and will make us even more confident that “purge mode” will work even if PLCs become unresponsive.
AWS-NRT-2019:S5: The overheating was due to a control system failure that caused multiple, redundant cooling systems to fail in parts of the affected Availability Zone.
AZ-AUE-2023:S113: Incremental load increases over time in the Availability Zone resulted in a chiller operating configuration that was susceptible to a timing defect in the Chiller Management System.
AZ-AUE-2023:S114: We have de-risked this failure to restart due to voltage fluctuations, by implementing a change to the control timing logic on the Chiller Management System (Completed).
AZ-AUE-2023:S115: Emergency Operation Procedure for manual restarts of simultaneous chiller failures has changed from an ‘adjacent’ sequence to a data hall ‘load based’ sequence to ensure all impacted data halls have partial cooling, to slow thermal runaway while full cooling is being restored (Completed).
AZ-AUE-2023:S116: Following this incident, as a temporary mitigation, we increased technician staffing levels at the datacenter to be prepared to execute manual restart procedures of our chillers prior to the change to the Chiller Management System to prevent restart failures.
AZ-AUE-2023:S117: Based on our incident analysis the staffing levels at the time would have been sufficient to prevent impact if a ‘load based' chiller restart sequence had been followed, which we have since implemented (Completed).
AZ-AUE-2023:S12: Starting at approximately 08:41 UTC on 30 August 2023, a utility voltage sag was caused by a lightning strike on electrical infrastructure approximately 18 miles from the impacted Availability Zone of the Australia East region.
AZ-AUE-2023:S13: The voltage sag caused cooling system chillers for multiple datacenters to shut down.
AZ-AUE-2023:S133: Our incident management team is exploring ways to harden our readiness, process, and playbook surrounding power down scenarios (Estimated completion: October 2023)
AZ-AUE-2023:S14: While some chillers automatically restarted, 13 failed to restart and required manual intervention.
AZ-AUE-2023:S15: To do so, the onsite team accessed the datacenter rooftop facilities, where the chillers are located, and proceeded to sequentially restart chillers moving from one datacenter to the next.
AZ-AUE-2023:S16: By the time the team reached the final five chillers requiring a manual restart, the water inside the pump system for these chillers (chilled water loop) had reached temperatures that were too high to allow them to be restarted.
AZ-AUE-2023:S17: In this scenario, the restart is inhibited by a self-protection mechanism that acts to prevent damage to the chiller that would occur by processing water at the elevated temperatures.
AZ-AUE-2023:S18: The five chillers that could not be restarted supported cooling for the two adjacent data halls which were impacted in this incident.
AZ-AUE-2023:S19: The two impacted data halls require at least four chillers to be operational.
AZ-AUE-2023:S20: Before the voltage sag, our cooling capacity for these halls consisted of seven chillers, with five chillers in operation and two chillers in standby.
AZ-AUE-2023:S21: At 10:30 UTC some networking, compute, and storage infrastructure began to shutdown automatically as data hall temperatures increased, impacting service availability.
AZ-AUE-2023:S22: At 11:34 UTC, as temperatures continued to increase, our onsite datacenter team began a remote shutdown of remaining networking, compute, and storage infrastructure in the impacted data halls to protect data durability, infrastructure health, and address the thermal runaway.
AZ-AUE-2023:S23: This shutdown allowed the chilled water loop to return to a safe temperature which allowed us to restart the chillers.
AZ-AUE-2023:S24: This shutdown of infrastructure resulted in a further reduction of service availability for this Availability Zone.
AZ-AUE-2023:S25: The chillers were successfully brought back online at 12:12 UTC, and data hall temperatures returned to operational thresholds by 13:30 UTC.
AZ-AUE-2023:S6: This incident was triggered by a utility power sag at 08:41 UTC on 30 August 2023, which impacted one of the three Availability Zones of the Australia East region.
AZ-AUE-2023:S7: This power sag tripped a subset of the cooling system chiller units offline and, while working to restore cooling, temperatures in the datacenter increased to levels above operational thresholds.

AZ-SCUS-2018:S10: Initially, the datacenter was able to maintain its operational temperatures through a load dependent thermal buffer that was designed within the cooling system.
AZ-SCUS-2018:S11: However, once this thermal buffer was depleted the datacenter temperature exceeded safe operational thresholds, and an automated shutdown of devices was initiated.
AZ-SCUS-2018:S12: This shutdown mechanism is intended to preserve infrastructure and data integrity, but in this instance, temperatures increased so quickly in parts of the datacenter that some hardware was damaged before it could shut down.
AZ-SCUS-2018:S13: A significant number of storage servers were damaged, as well as a small number of network devices and power units.
AZ-SCUS-2018:S14: While storms were still active in the area, onsite teams took a series of actions to prevent further damage – including transferring the rest of the datacenter to generators thereby stabilizing the power supply.
AZ-SCUS-2018:S21: Despite onsite redundancies, there are scenarios in which a datacenter cooling failure can impact customer workloads in the affected datacenter.
AZ-SCUS-2018:S25: Customer impact began at approximately 09:29 UTC when storage servers in the datacenter began shutting down as a result of unsafe temperatures.
AZ-SCUS-2018:S5: Summary of impact: In the early morning of September 4, 2018, high energy storms hit southern Texas in the vicinity of Microsoft Azure’s South Central US region.
AZ-SCUS-2018:S6: Multiple Azure datacenters in the region saw voltage sags and swells across the utility feeds.
AZ-SCUS-2018:S7: At 08:42 UTC, lightning caused electrical activity on the utility supply, which caused significant voltage swells.
AZ-SCUS-2018:S8: These swells triggered a portion of one Azure datacenter to transfer from utility power to generator power.

AZ-SCUS-2018:S84: 3. An evaluation of the future hardware design of storage scale units to increase resiliency to environmental factors.
AZ-SCUS-2018:S85: In addition, for scenarios in which impact is unavoidable, we are determining software changes to automate and accelerate recovery.

EQX-SIN-2023:S1: On October 14, DBS and Citibank suffered an IT outage that affected millions of payment transactions in Singapore.
EQX-SIN-2023:S10: The two financial institutions didn't comply with the requirements from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) related to resilience of critical IT systems.
EQX-SIN-2023:S11: MAS dictates that unscheduled downtime for critical banking systems should not exceed four hours within a 12-month period, and the October issue clearly went beyond that limit.
EQX-SIN-2023:S4: The October outage resulted in full or partial unavailability of the online banking services provided by DBS and Citibank, Minister Alvin Tan confirmed during a parliamentary Q&A session.
EQX-SIN-2023:S5: The root cause of the issue was later identified in a non-functioning cooling system at the Equinix data center used by both banks, which made the server temperatures rise above optimal operating conditions.
EQX-SIN-2023:S6: The outage led to 810,000 failed access attempts, Tan said this Monday, with 2.5 million unsuccessful payment and ATM transactions.
EQX-SIN-2023:S7: According to Equinix, the overheating issue was caused by a contractor that sent an incorrect signal to "close the valves from the chilled water buffer tanks" during a planned system upgrade.
EQX-SIN-2023:S8: DBS and Citibank had some backup plans prepared for this kind of situation, but those turned out to be absolutely worthless.
EQX-SIN-2023:S9: DBS was unable to reach its backup data center because of a "network misconfiguration," Singapore's government said, while Citibank had some unspecified connectivity issues.

GCP-LDN-2022:S31: We powered down this part of the zone to prevent an even longer outage or damage to machines.
GCP-LDN-2022:S34: Google engineers were alerted to an issue affecting two cooling systems in one of the data centers that hosts europe-west2-a on Tuesday, 19 July 2022 at 06:33 US/Pacific and began an investigation.
GCP-LDN-2022:S35: Engineers were engaged at 07:02 and began assessing viable mitigations.

GCP-LDN-2022:S42: We will investigate and develop more advanced methods to progressively decrease the thermal load within a single data center space, reducing the probability that a full shutdown is required.
GCP-LDN-2022:S46: Google engineers are actively conducting a detailed analysis of the cooling system failure that triggered this incident.
